processing: A flavoured blend: black tea scented with bergamot, typically with added citrus peel, lemongrass and cornflower petals. Recipes differ from one blender to the next.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; blended all year from black teas of various origins.
appearance_dry: Dark black leaf flecked with orange peel, pale lemongrass and blue cornflower petals.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish amber, as with most bergamot-scented black teas.
appearance_wet: Soft dark leaf with softened peel and faded petals.
taste_profile: Bergamot over plain black tea with a sharper, brighter citrus edge from peel and lemongrass; the base usually stays in the background.

brewing.notes: Brew Western-style. Long steeps push the peel toward bitterness, so start short. The usual Earl Grey caution applies: a strongly scented blend can taste perfumed when very hot.

vintage_note: Sold as a year-round blend without harvest or vintage dates, typically with a best-before date only. Scent fades faster than tea, so buy small amounts and keep them sealed. Check the ingredient list, because the name covers quite different recipes.
description:
Russian Earl Grey is a commercial variation on Earl Grey: black tea and bergamot with extra citrus. There is no fixed definition. Versions on sale commonly add citrus peel, lemongrass and cornflower petals.

The extras change the character more than the look suggests. Lemongrass and peel add a tangy brightness on top of bergamot's softer perfume, while cornflower is mostly there for colour.

As with other flavoured blends, the scent leads and the tea base supports. Brew it like Earl Grey and keep an eye on the time, since peel can turn bitter in a long steep.

When buying, read the ingredients rather than the name, and look for whether the flavouring is natural or synthetic. The word Russian is a selling label here, not a place of origin: these blends are made by tea companies in many countries.
history:
Little is documented about where the name began or who first used it. It appears as a product name among Western tea sellers, and no firm date or link to any Russian tea tradition has been established.

The parent blend is better recorded: bergamot-flavoured tea is mentioned from 1824, and the Earl Grey name appears in advertisements of the 1880s.
